chapters.title: Chapter 1: Two Families of Assets, One Question

lessons.title: Traditional vs Alternative Assets: Where the Line Actually Falls

children.text: Two friends in Bengaluru each have ₹10 lakh to invest. Ananya splits hers between a Nifty 50 index fund on Zerodha Coin and a gold ETF. Kabir puts all of his into a fractional share of a pre-leased office in Whitefield through an online platform, because someone told him it was time to "go alternative." A year later, Ananya can see the exact value of her holdings every evening and sell before lunch the next day. Kabir gets an occasional valuation from the platform, and he can exit only if another investor agrees to buy his share or the building is sold. Both of them own real things. Only one of them owns something that behaves like an alternative asset. This lesson gives you the test for telling the two apart.

body.text: "Alternative" is not a kind of asset. It is a set of behaviours: how the asset is bought, how it is priced and how easily you can get out. The same office building can be a traditional holding in one wrapper and an alternative one in another.

children.text: What Counts as Traditional
In an Indian portfolio, traditional assets are the ones most households and advisers already build around:
Equity.
Shares listed on NSE and BSE, plus the equity mutual funds and ETFs that hold them.
Debt.
Bank FDs, government securities, listed corporate bonds, debt mutual funds and small savings schemes like PPF.
Cash.
Savings accounts and liquid funds.
Gold.

This course treats gold as traditional. Indian families have held it for generations, and gold ETFs trade on NSE like any share. Global textbooks often file gold under alternatives, so expect to see both labels.
What these assets share is not safety. A small-cap stock can halve in a year. What they share is
structure

: a public market or a tightly regulated product, a price you can check every day, low minimums, standard disclosures and a quick way out. Shares sold on NSE or BSE settle on the next trading day, and mutual funds must pay redemption proceeds within three working days.

body.label: Equity settlement cycle in India
body.context: Shares sold on NSE or BSE today are settled on the next trading day. Most alternative assets take weeks, months or years to turn into cash.

children.text: The Six Traits of an Alternative Asset
An asset starts behaving like an alternative when it shows several of these traits. One trait on its own does not settle it. The more traits it has, the further along the scale it sits.
No active exchange.
It is bought and sold privately, or on a market so thin that finding a buyer takes real effort.

markDefs.definition: Valuing an asset using a valuer's estimate, a manager's model or recent comparable deals, instead of a price set by continuous trading.

children.text: Appraisal pricing.
Its value comes from
appraisal-based pricing
: a valuer, a fund manager's model or the last deal done, not trades happening every second.
Lock-ins and slow exits.
You may be contractually locked in for years, or free to sell but unable to find a buyer at a fair price.
High minimums.
Tickets of ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore or more force you to concentrate a large share of your money in one bet.
Manager and deal dependence.
The return depends heavily on who picks the deals. Two Nifty 50 index funds deliver almost identical returns. Two venture capital funds from the same year can deliver wildly different ones.
Lighter disclosure.
Reports are fewer and less frequent, and there is usually no independent daily price to check them against.

children.text: The Wrapper Test: Same Asset, Different Behaviour
This is where most confusion starts. The underlying asset does not decide whether your holding is traditional or alternative. The wrapper does.

body.caption: Same underlying asset, two very different experiences

cells: Listed REIT units, such as Embassy Office Parks REIT, bought on NSE
A fractional share of one office building through a platform, or an office unit bought outright
Gold ETF units on NSE, sold in seconds
Jewellery or coins in a bank locker, sold to a jeweller at a deduction
Unlisted or pre-IPO shares bought through a dealer
A debt mutual fund or a listed corporate bond
A P2P loan or a private credit AIF

children.text: Swiggy is a clean example. Before its IPO in November 2024, its shares changed hands in the unlisted market through dealers: no exchange price, wide gaps between buying and selling quotes, and manual off-market transfers. The day it listed on NSE and BSE, the same share in the same company picked up every traditional trait at once: a live price, a fast exit and regular public disclosure. The business did not change overnight. The wrapper did.

body.text: A listed REIT owns office parks, which sounds alternative. But its units trade on NSE, so their price moves every day and can swing with market sentiment like any listed share. Chapter 4 looks at how much of a REIT's behaviour is real estate and how much is stock market.

body.title: The cost of a thin market
body.prompt: A dealer offers to sell you a pre-IPO share at ₹500 and to buy it back from you at ₹450. If you buy one share and immediately change your mind, what percentage of your money do you lose on the round trip? Ignore taxes and fees.
body.explanation: (₹500 minus ₹450) ÷ ₹500 = 10%. A large-cap stock like Reliance Industries usually trades on NSE with a gap of just a few paise between the best buy and sell quotes, a tiny fraction of 1%. That gap is one of the hidden costs of alternative assets, and it never shows up in a headline return figure.

children.text: A Spectrum, Not a Switch
Stop thinking in two boxes. Every holding sits somewhere on a line from fully traditional to deeply alternative, and the time it takes to turn into cash is the quickest way to place it.

body.title: Spot the most alternative holding
body.question: Which of these holdings shows the MOST alternative traits?
options: Units of Embassy Office Parks REIT bought on NSE
A gold ETF held in a Zerodha demat account
A ₹25 lakh investment in a seed-stage startup through an angel fund
A five-year fixed deposit with SBI
body.explanation: The startup stake has almost every trait: no exchange, an estimated value, a likely exit horizon of 5 to 10 years, a large ticket and heavy dependence on which startups were picked. The REIT owns an alternative underlying asset but trades like a share. The gold ETF and the FD are traditional.

children.text: Why the Label Matters Before You Compare Returns

This is not a naming exercise. The traits above change what the numbers mean. When a Nifty 50 index fund shows a return, it is built on prices that thousands of buyers and sellers actually agreed on. When a colleague says their Pune flat, bought for ₹80 lakh in 2019, is "now worth ₹1.3 crore," that is a broker's estimate. Nobody has paid it yet, and the brokerage, the months of waiting and the effort needed to actually collect it are not in the number.
Putting those two figures side by side as if they were the same kind of number is the most common mistake investors make with alternatives. The rest of this course is about comparing them properly.

body.title: Sort the Mehta family portfolio
body.scenario: The Mehtas in Pune hold six things: (a) ₹40 lakh in equity mutual funds, (b) a second flat in Wakad they estimate at ₹85 lakh, (c) ₹15 lakh in listed REIT units, (d) ₹10 lakh in a fractional share of a warehouse through an online platform, (e) ₹8 lakh of gold jewellery, and (f) ₹12 lakh in PPF.
body.prompt: Label each holding traditional, hybrid or alternative, and name the one trait that decided it. Then work out roughly what share of the family's total sits in alternatives.
body.modelAnswer:
(a) Equity mutual funds: traditional. Daily NAV and redemption within 3 working days.
(b) Wakad flat: alternative. The ₹85 lakh is an estimate, and a sale could take months.
(c) Listed REIT units: hybrid. The underlying is real estate, but the units trade daily on NSE.
(d) Fractional warehouse share: alternative. One building, a platform valuation, and an exit that depends on finding another buyer.
(e) Gold jewellery: hybrid. Gold is priced daily, but selling means a jeweller's deduction.
(f) PPF: traditional, despite its 15-year tenure. Nobody estimates its value, the government sets the rate each quarter, and there is no manager or deal risk. A lock-in on its own does not make an asset alternative.

Total: ₹40 + ₹85 + ₹15 + ₹10 + ₹8 + ₹12 = ₹170 lakh. Alternatives: ₹85 + ₹10 = ₹95 lakh, or about 56%. Most of that is one flat, which is exactly the kind of concentration Chapter 6 deals with.

body.title: Name the pricing method
body.textWithBlank: When an asset's value comes from a valuer's estimate instead of continuous trading, it is said to use ___ pricing.
body.explanation: Appraisal pricing is the hallmark of real estate, private equity, private credit and most other alternatives. Chapter 2 shows how it makes these assets look calmer than they really are.

cards.definition: Listed equity, debt, cash and, in this course, gold: priced daily, easy to exit, low minimums, standard disclosure.
A holding that shows several of these traits: no active exchange, appraisal pricing, slow exits, high minimums, manager dependence and lighter disclosure.
Value set by a valuer, a manager's model or recent deals, rather than by continuous trading.
The form in which you hold an underlying asset, such as a listed REIT unit versus a directly owned office. The wrapper, not the asset, decides the behaviour.
An asset with an alternative underlying but a traditional wrapper, such as listed REIT units.

points: "Traditional" and "alternative" describe how an asset behaves, not what it is or how safe it is.
Six traits mark an alternative: no active exchange, appraisal pricing, slow exits, high minimums, manager and deal dependence, and lighter disclosure.
The wrapper decides the behaviour. Office buildings are hybrid inside a listed REIT and alternative when owned directly.
Assets sit on a spectrum, and time to cash is the quickest way to place them.
A lock-in alone does not make an asset alternative. PPF is locked for 15 years and is still traditional.
Returns from appraised, illiquid assets are not the same kind of number as returns from listed markets, so never compare them side by side without adjusting.
